description:
🔥 Team QABAS

Qabas (قبس) means “a spark of fire” in Arabic. We are engineering and science students passionate about space safety. Fire behaves differently in microgravity, creating unique risks. Our AI-powered dashboard transforms NASA’s research into clear, accessible insights to improve fire safety in space.
summary:
QABAS is a web dashboard for NASA’s spacecraft fire data. It lists the seventeen combustion investigations named in the challenge and groups them by fire safety pillar. So far only SAFFIRE-II has its full data in the site, because it was the only dataset we could get in time. We went through its NASA Physical Sciences Informatics record, sensor files and camera images included, and put every test into tables where each value links back to its source file.

You can browse the nine samples SAFFIRE-II burned inside a Cygnus spacecraft in 2016. The 3D Fire Lab replays each burn second by second next to the same sample’s result on Earth. Four of the nine samples burned completely on Earth but not in microgravity. SAFFIRE-II only tested normal cabin air, so for other oxygen levels, pressures and airflows the lab shows what published experiments found with sources. Ask QABAS takes a plain-language question and returns the matching records.

Spacecraft materials are screened with tests on Earth, and those results do not always hold in orbit. One investigation cannot tell us about fire on the Moon or Mars, so the next step is full data for BASS, FLEX and the rest.
details:
What it does

QABAS puts NASA’s spacecraft fire experiments in one place.

The site opens with a short animated story, drawn as a single continuous line, showing how a small fire can become dangerous when its behaviour is not understood.

The first page lists the seventeen combustion investigations named in the challenge, grouped under prevention, detection, suppression and supporting science. Pick what you need to know, such as choosing cabin materials or detecting a fire, and the list is ranked by relevance.

One investigation, SAFFIRE-II, has its full data in the site. In 2016 it burned nine material samples inside a Cygnus cargo spacecraft. For each sample you can see the test conditions, the result in microgravity beside the result on Earth, the sensor peaks, and the places where NASA’s own documents disagree.

The Fire Lab replays each burn second by second. A 3D view lets you orbit the sample while the flame moves along it, with the temperature, CO2, oxygen and radiometer readings for that second. A separate set of controls for oxygen, pressure, airflow and diluent gas shows what other published experiments found at those settings. Those results are labelled as coming from outside SAFFIRE-II, and each one names its source.

The insights page ranks the four materials by how far they burned and lists the four samples that burned completely on Earth but not in microgravity.

Ask QABAS uses Gemini to turn a question into a search across our database tables. It shows only the matching records, each with its original source. It does not generate answers from information outside the data.

How it works

NASA publishes SAFFIRE-II as spreadsheets, documents and tens of thousands of camera images. We wrote Python scripts to read the sensor workbooks, which hold about 30 readings per second. The scripts find when the igniter switched on, subtract each radiometer’s resting offset and average the data to one reading per second. To get flame position we tracked the glowing region in one camera frame per second and converted pixels to centimetres with NASA’s calibration grids. Our figure for the cotton-fiberglass sample came out at 2.04 mm/s against NASA’s reported 2.1 mm/s.

A FastAPI backend serves the tables. The front end is React, and the 3D lab is drawn with Three.js.

What we considered

We kept to what the data supports. Where two NASA documents give different values for a sample’s thickness or airflow, the site shows both. Missing values stay blank. Labels we added ourselves, such as “partial burn”, are marked as ours.

Every SAFFIRE-II test ran in normal cabin air at about 20 cm/s airflow. The site says so, and it tells the reader not to use these results to predict fire in a lunar or Martian habitat.

Why it matters

Spacecraft materials are screened with flammability tests on Earth. SAFFIRE-II shows that the result can change in orbit: two silicone samples that burned completely on Earth did not spread flame at all in microgravity. QABAS lets a designer or a student see that in the measured data and follow any number back to its NASA file. Next we want to add full data for BASS, FLEX and the other investigations, which would bring in more materials, oxygen levels and pressures.

What is new about it

The Fire Lab is a replay of a real space fire built from NASA’s own sensors and cameras, shown next to the same sample’s result on Earth. We could not find flame position over time in the published tables, so we measured it from the images.

Tools

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML/CSS
  • Frameworks and libraries: FastAPI, pandas, React, Vite, Three.js
  • AI: Google Gemini API (gemini-2.5-flash) for the Ask QABAS search; ChatGPT and Claude for coding help, data extraction and building the Fire Lab
  • Hosting: Vercel (site), Render (API), GitHub (code)
  • Design: Claude, for the video demo.
